newsitem.title: USA: HP says court accepts InkJet package plan.
newsitem.headline: HP says court accepts InkJet package plan.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co said Wednesday a federal judge has accepted its proposal for revising packaging of two popular black InkJet cartridges and it greatly reduced its estimated cost for the changes.

Hewlett-Packard also said federal court Judge James Ware had "rebuffed all remedies" proposed by Nu-kote International Inc, which originally brought the action, and required Nu-Kote post $75,000 bond against any harm the packaging change may have caused HP.

A company spokesman said Hewlett-Packard had also greatly reduced its estimate of the cost of modyfying an illustration on the cartridge packaging to $440,000 from its original estimate last week of $3 million to $6 million.
The ruling in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California in San Jose follows a ruling the judge made on a preliminary injunction motion by Nu-kote.

Nu-Kote, which markets ink that can be injected into older-style HP cartridges, had asked the court to stop HP from making a new design of the popular "26A and "29A" InkJet cartridges because a so-called top ink-fill hole was removed.
The cartridges -- formally dubbed the 51626A and 51629A -- are used in a variety of printing devices, including DeskJet printers and OfficeJet multifunction and fax machines.

Nu-Kote had argued that Hewlett-Packard was unfairly restricting competition by eliminating the hole, which Nu-kote's products have utilized to enable customers to inject fresh ink into the cartridges.
In the previous ruling, Ware denied Nu-kote's request that HP be required to halt conversion of its manufacturing lines to a new bottom ink-fill format design for the cartridges.

HP said it designed the new bottom-fill cartridges to make them more reliable, a process which will take HP roughly 18 months from start to finish to complete. HP does not supply replacement ink and sells only replacement cartridges.

The decision Wednesday involved Nu-kote's claim that HP had mislabelled its packaging but shipping the older style cartridges, which have the top fill hole, in newer packaging which did not depict the fill hole.
Nu-kote had argued that the practice disguised cartridges still being sold which its customers could refill.
An HP spokesman said that in accepting HP's proposal to modify the illustrations, the judge said he believed HP had originally revised its packaging in good faith.
HP proposed that by September 30, 1997, it would begin U.S. shipments of its top-filled cartridges in packaging depicting the top fill hole.
Nu-kote's motion was part of ongoing litigation between the two companies. Hewlett-Packard originally sued Nu-Kote for patent infringement and Nu-Kote filed a counterclaim on anti-trust grounds.
